strengths: The paper is clearly written and the method (retrieval of high-return target states + step-estimated condition-guided diffusion planning) is described with enough architectural detail to follow, including the pseudo-target training strategy and conditioning format.

Ablation studies (retrieval vs. random target sampling, fixed vs. variable target position, random vs. learned step estimation) and a hyperparameter study over top-k and similarity threshold are provided and show each component matters.
The authors honestly discuss limitations, including the failure on HalfCheetah and the dependence of retrieval on dataset coverage.
Evaluation covers a standard suite of D4RL MuJoCo tasks with reasonable baselines (BC, DT, TT, Diffuser, DD, DS, CEIL, ReDiffuser) and reports standard deviations.
weaknesses: The central claims are not supported by the evidence. The abstract and contributions claim 'competitive or superior performance,' yet Table 1 shows RAD's average (81.2) is below ReDiffuser (82.6) and DD (81.8), and it is the worst near-top method on HalfCheetah across all three dataset types. The claimed advantage — better generalization to OOD/underrepresented states — is never directly tested: there is no OOD evaluation, no AntMaze (the canonical stitching benchmark), no Locomotion-v2/Adroit/Kitchen, only 9 MuJoCo tasks.

The motivation (adaptive stitching beyond static augmentation) does not match the training procedure. Training conditions the diffusion model on a pseudo target st+i drawn from the same trajectory (Eq. 13–14), so the model never learns to stitch between disconnected trajectories; at inference it must generalize to retrieved targets from other trajectories, a train/inference mismatch that is not analyzed. This also makes the method close to existing goal-conditioned diffusion planning (e.g., SfBC, Hierarchical Diffuser), which are not compared against or cited, limiting demonstrated novelty over prior work.

The return-guidance model J_phi in Eq. 7 is central to the generative process but its training is never specified — Eq. 14 trains only the denoiser. The guidance scale rho, tolerance eta, horizon H, and similarity threshold delta defaults are also under-specified, hurting reproducibility; no code release is mentioned.

The retrieval mechanism is extremely naive: raw-state cosine similarity on MuJoCo state vectors (with heterogeneous units/scales) with a hard threshold delta=0.9. No learned embeddings or distance metrics are explored, and the parameter study shows high sensitivity (Walker2d-Medium swings from 64.3 to 82.8), suggesting brittleness rather than robust 'dynamic adaptation.'

Statistical rigor is weak: only 3 random seeds, with very large variance in some cells (Hopper-Medium 82.5±12.7), and no significance analysis. Conclusions about outperforming baselines cannot be drawn at this sample size.

The step estimation module is trained to predict offsets to uniformly sampled pseudo-targets within trajectories (Eq. 15), but at inference it must predict steps to retrieved external targets whose distance distribution differs; this distribution shift is unaddressed. Writing also needs polish (e.g., Section 4.2 lowercase title, 'targe states', inconsistent use of N for both dataset size and denoising steps, imprecise discounted-return definition in Section 3).

The 'static vs. dynamic augmentation' distinction is overstated: recent augmentation methods (e.g., SynthER) already generate data adaptively during training, and the comparison to augmentation baselines is narrative rather than empirical — no trajectory-augmentation baseline is actually run.

strengths: The paper is clearly motivated and well-organized: the retrieval + step-estimation + condition-guided diffusion decomposition ('where to go' / 'how long to get there') is intuitive and easy to follow, supported by a helpful motivating figure.

The ablation study (Figure 3) and parameter study (Table 2) are reasonably thorough, showing that each component (retrieval, variable target sampling, step estimation) contributes, and the training-curve comparison in Figure 4 suggests retrieval also stabilizes training.
The limitations section is honest, correctly identifying that retrieval depends on reachable high-value states existing in the dataset and that RAD performs local, per-decision retrieval.
The method is simple and modular, which aids reproducibility of the core idea even without released code.
weaknesses: The central claim — that retrieval-guided generation improves generalization to out-of-distribution/underrepresented states — is never directly tested. The evaluation consists only of standard D4RL MuJoCo tasks (HalfCheetah, Hopper, Walker2d), where the agent is not evaluated from novel or OOD start states. Benchmarks specifically designed for stitching/generalization (e.g., AntMaze, FrankaKitchen, or controlled OOD-start evaluations) are absent, so the motivating Figure 1 scenario is never instantiated experimentally.

The main results do not support 'competitive or superior performance': RAD's average (81.2) is below ReDiffuser (82.6) and DD (81.8), and it underperforms on several tasks (e.g., HalfCheetah across all three dataset types, Medium Walker2d vs. DD). The headline contribution therefore rests on the untested generalization claim.

The experimental evidence is statistically weak: only 3 random seeds, with very high variance in places (Hopper-Medium: 82.5±12.7; Table 2 shows variances up to ±23.7). No significance tests are reported, and differences of a few normalized points on 3 seeds are not interpretable.

Several technical elements are underspecified or inconsistent: the return-guidance function J_ϕ in Eq. (7) is introduced at inference but its architecture, training objective, and relationship to the training losses in Section 4.4 are never described; how anchors are held fixed across denoising steps is not detailed; the 'pseudo target strategy' means training only ever conditions on within-trajectory targets, which is not obviously consistent with the cross-trajectory stitching performed at inference.

The methodological novelty is limited: retrieval of high-return states plus guided diffusion is a straightforward combination of existing ingredients (Diffuser/DD-style trajectory diffusion, retrieval-augmented generation, and goal-conditioning), and the paper does not clearly differentiate RAD from prior retrieval-based or goal-conditioned offline RL methods beyond a brief related-work treatment.

No code or reproducibility materials are mentioned; hyperparameters beyond a few (H=32, 20 denoising steps, k=6, δ=0.9) are unspecified (network size, training iterations, learning rates), hindering reproduction.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a main-track submission: repeated phrasing errors ('retrieving high-return target states as target states'), lowercase section heading ('target selection module'), typos ('targe states'), inconsistent notation (subscripts t vs. i in Eq. 14), and the vague claim that static augmentation methods 'cannot adapt when the agent encounters new states during deployment' despite the setting being fully offline.

The sensitivity analysis (Table 2) actually reveals brittleness that undercuts the robustness narrative: performance collapses for many (k, δ) settings (e.g., Walker2d-Medium drops from 82.8 to 46-58), yet the text frames the best configuration as evidence of effectiveness without discussing how sensitive the method is to tuning.

strengths: The paper is well motivated: the distinction between static, pre-generated data augmentation and decision-time retrieval-guided planning is clearly articulated and illustrated (Figure 1), and the proposed framework (retrieval of high-return target states + condition-guided diffusion with a step estimation anchor) is coherent and easy to follow.

The method is described at a level of detail sufficient to reimplement: the database structure, retrieval scoring, return filtering, step estimation loss, and diffusion training with pseudo-targets are all specified (Sections 4.2–4.4).

The evaluation includes component ablations (retrieval, conditional diffusion conditioning, step estimation), training-curve comparisons with/without retrieval (Figure 4), and a hyperparameter study over the similarity threshold and top-k selection (Table 2).

The limitations section is honest: the authors explicitly acknowledge dependence on dataset coverage of reachable high-value states, potential retrieval failure in noisy/stochastic settings, and purely local per-decision retrieval.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is not supported. The abstract and contributions claim 'competitive or superior performance' and 'superiority of RAD', but Table 1 shows RAD's average normalized return (81.2) is below ReDiffuser (82.6) and DD (81.8), and RAD is not best on the majority of tasks. The results actually support 'matches but does not outperform' stronger baselines.

The core motivation — improved generalization to out-of-distribution states and flexible trajectory stitching (Figures 1(c), 1(d)) — is never directly evaluated. All experiments are standard D4RL MuJoCo in-distribution tasks; there is no OOD perturbation study, no stitching benchmark (e.g., AntMaze or maze environments where stitching is the operative challenge), and no quantitative demonstration that RAD's dynamic retrieval actually succeeds where static augmentation fails. The paper's headline claim remains untested.

The evaluation scope is narrow: only 9 MuJoCo tasks (3 environments × 3 dataset types), with 3 random seeds. High-variance results (e.g., Hopper-Medium 82.5±12.7) make several per-task comparisons statistically inconclusive at this seed count.

The paper criticizes trajectory augmentation baselines (SER, single-way rollout methods) in Related Work, but never empirically compares against them, so the claimed advantage over static augmentation is asserted rather than shown.

The results reveal severe sensitivity to retrieval hyperparameters: in Table 2, changing k from 6 to 30 collapses Walker2d-Medium from 82.8 to 46.1, and the similarity threshold δ has swings of 20–30 points. This brittleness undercuts the claim of robust dynamic retrieval and is only briefly acknowledged.

Methodological novelty is modest: retrieval of goal states plus goal-conditioned diffusion planning is close to existing stitching and goal-conditioned diffusion approaches (e.g., CEIL, Diffuser-style conditioning). The retrieval itself uses raw cosine similarity on states rather than learned embeddings, and no theoretical or empirical analysis is provided for when retrieval-guided stitching should succeed.

Presentation issues reduce clarity: inconsistent section header capitalization ('4.2 target selection module'), typos ('targe states', 'policy'’s'), a garbled sentence fragment at the end of Section 3, and ablation results relegated to figures with unlabeled axes (Figure 3) rather than reported numerically.

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned, several implementation details are missing (architecture of the return predictor Jϕ, how return guidance is trained, how anchors are enforced during denoising), and baselines are largely cited from prior reports rather than re-run under a uniform protocol.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning D4RL (MuJoCo, AntMaze, FrankaKitchen, Maze2D) and OGBench, with broad baselines including imitation, model-free, model-based, return-conditioned, augmentation-based, and diffusion-planning methods

Extensive ablations that specifically test each component (TS, SE, pseudo-target strategy), including ablations separating retrieval benefits from expert-subset filtering (Table 18) and from naive retrieval injection (Table 8, DRC baseline), which strengthen the causal claim that the retrieval-guided design matters

Strong results on the core motivating setting: distribution-shift evaluations (Tables 2, 3, 11) show DL-RAD succeeding where baselines score 0.0, which directly supports the central claim about OOD generalization

Thorough sensitivity and robustness analyses in the appendix: sensitivity to similarity threshold, similarity metric, degraded retrieval ranking, periodic replanning for inference cost, and per-step latency measurements

Honest limitations discussion in the conclusion acknowledging dependence on dataset coverage and limited environment diversity; reproducibility is aided by code release, algorithm pseudocode, and hyperparameter details
weaknesses: Overstated novelty: the claim of 'innovatively introducing a retrieval mechanism into offline RL' is not well supported. Retrieval-augmented decision-making/planning (e.g., RAP, Yang et al., 2023) and planning-toward-high-return-states methods (notably ContraDiff, Shan et al., ICLR 2024, which is cited in the references but never discussed or compared) are closely related and absent from the related work. The core idea — retrieve high-value states and condition a generative planner on them — appears to be a combination of existing ideas rather than a fundamentally new understanding

Mixed headline results weaken the generality claim: D-RAD performs poorly on AntMaze (e.g., 13.3 vs. DiffuserLite's 72.0 on AntMaze-Large, 6.7 vs. 92.4 on AntMaze-Medium-Diverse) and below strong baselines on several MuJoCo tasks (e.g., 84.9 vs. DD's 95.7 on HalfCheetah-ME). The paper's claim of 'best or near-best on 16 of 18 datasets' is only true for one of the two variants, and the failure of D-RAD is not adequately explained
Only 3 random seeds with no significance testing, despite several reported margins (e.g., 3 points on Walker-Medium-Replay) being within typical seed variance for these benchmarks

Some technical presentation issues: the 'expert trajectory' database construction is defined by environment-specific heuristics that feel ad hoc; Eq. (9) and the surrounding diffusion notation contain inconsistencies; the appendix has duplicate section labeling ('E.' appears twice); minor typos ('Visulization', 'targe states', 'difficult than classification')

The appendix entropy-reduction 'proof' (Appendix E) is a trivial consequence of the chain rule of mutual information and provides little actual insight into why the method works; presenting it as theoretical support overstates its value

Similarity metrics (cosine similarity on raw states, Euclidean distance on 2D positions) are brittle choices for high-dimensional states; while a metric sensitivity study exists, no learned-state-representation alternative is explored, limiting the scope of the retrieval mechanism

strengths: The paper tackles a genuine and well-motivated problem: generalization beyond the support of static offline datasets, and the dynamic (per-step) retrieval of targets is a sensible alternative to static data augmentation approaches such as SER and DiffStitch.
The experimental scope is broad: D4RL (MuJoCo, AntMaze, Kitchen, Maze2D), a modified OOD evaluation protocol, and additional results on OGBench stitching/explore settings.

The ablation suite is unusually thorough: component ablations (-TS, -TSR, -SE, -PTS), comparison with a naive retrieval variant (DRC, Table 8), expert-subset-filtering control (Table 18), sensitivity to retrieval ranking noise (Table 12), similarity metric choice (Table 13), and a thoughtful computational cost analysis including periodic replanning (Tables 14-15).

The region-restricted AntMaze experiments (Table 3) directly probe the central claim about OOD generalization, and the 20%-coverage results (e.g., 47.8 on AntMaze-Large-Play) are striking relative to baselines.
The paper is candid in its limitations discussion: it acknowledges dependence on dataset coverage and that D-RAD underperforms on Medium-Expert datasets.
weaknesses: The empirical results are much less consistent than the abstract and contribution claims suggest. The claim of 'best or near-best performance on 16 out of 18 datasets' is misleading: D-RAD collapses on AntMaze (e.g., 40.0 vs. DiffuserLite's 78.0 on AntMaze-Medium-Play; 6.7-26.7 on the other AntMaze tasks) and Maze2D-Large D-RAD (149.2) is accompanied by DL-RAD at only 44.3. The two variants diverge wildly across suites (e.g., Kitchen: DL-RAD 72.1 but D-RAD 64.2, below DiffuserLite's 74.0; Maze2d average 134.9 vs 66.9), suggesting the mechanism is fragile and its benefit is highly variant- and task-dependent. The manuscript does not adequately explain or confront this inconsistency.

Only 3 random seeds are used, with visibly large standard errors on the tasks where the method is weakest (e.g., D-RAD 13.3±3.6 on AntMaze-Large-Play). Given the fragility noted above, this is insufficient evidence for the headline claims.

Novelty is moderate and the framing overstates it. Retrieving high-value/goal states from the dataset and planning toward them is closely related to existing goal-conditioned and value-guided planning methods (Contradiff is cited as 'planning towards high-return states'; HIQL, CRL, and retrieval-augmented planners are directly comparable in Table 17). The claim of 'innovatively introduces a retrieval mechanism into offline RL' ignores prior retrieval-augmented decision-making work.

There is a tension in the OOD generalization narrative: retrieval requires similar states in the database, and Algorithm 2 explicitly falls back to the backbone planner when no candidate is found. Thus in the most truly OOD regimes the method degenerates to the baseline, which is consistent with the 0.0 score on AntMaze-Large-Play at 0% coverage (Table 3) — a result that undercuts the paper's central story but is not discussed critically.

The theoretical content is thin. Appendix E reduces to a standard chain-rule/conditional-mutual-information argument and provides no insight into when retrieval actually helps; it does not connect to the reachability or return properties that the method relies on.

The method requires privileged preprocessing: constructing an 'expert' database depends on heuristics that differ per environment (e.g., first-hitting-step thresholds in AntMaze, trajectory lengths in locomotion, per-maze step ranges in Maze2D, Appendix C). This complicates reproducibility and raises the question of how the method transfers to settings without such clean quality signals.

Writing quality is uneven: several grammatical errors ('which is difficult than classification'), a duplicated Appendix label (two sections labeled 'E'), and hyperparameter sensitivity results (Tables 9-10) show large, unexplained swings (e.g., Kitchen-M going from 0.0 at δ=0.6 to 72.7 at δ=0.9), which further undercuts the robustness narrative.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the paper covers D4RL (MuJoCo, AntMaze, Kitchen, Maze2D), OGBench stitching/explore settings, and multiple distribution-shift protocols (Tables 2, 3, 11), with a diverse set of baselines spanning imitation, model-free, model-based, and diffusion-based methods.

Extensive ablation and sensitivity analyses: the ablations (-TS, -TSR, -SE, -PTS; Tables 7, 16), the DRC comparison (Table 8) which cleanly shows the gains are not from naive retrieval injection, the expert-subset-filtering control (Table 18), retrieval-noise stress tests (Table 12), similarity-metric sensitivity (Table 13), and periodic-replanning cost analysis (Tables 14-15) collectively strengthen the credibility of the core claims.

The generalization experiments (region-restricted AntMaze training, Table 3) directly target the paper's central motivation and show meaningful advantages (e.g., 36.7-52.2 under coverage settings where all baselines score 0.0), which is more informative than standard benchmark numbers alone.

Honest limitations discussion: the conclusion explicitly acknowledges dependence on offline dataset coverage and limited visualization scope, and the appendix transparently reports worst-case retrieval latency and cases where the method underperforms (e.g., D-RAD on AntMaze, DL-RAD on Maze2D).
Computational cost is treated seriously rather than glossed over, with training time, per-step inference, memory footprint, and wall-clock measurements provided.
The method is presented as backbone-agnostic (footnote 1), and the source code is released, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: retrieving high-value/reachable states as subgoals and conditioning a generative planner on them is closely related to goal-conditioned diffusion planning, hindsight goal relabeling, and prior work on planning toward high-return states (e.g., ContraDiff, cited in the paper itself). The TS/SE modules are largely heuristic engineering (cosine similarity in raw state space, longest-remaining-trajectory tie-breaking) rather than a principled new learning mechanism. The entropy-reduction argument in Appendix E is a standard chain-rule identity and adds little explanatory power.

Inconsistent variant performance undermines the framework story: D-RAD collapses on AntMaze (21.7 average vs. 83.3 for DL-RAD, sometimes below plain DiffuserLite) and DL-RAD degrades sharply on Maze2D (66.9 vs. 134.9 for D-RAD and 119.5 for Diffuser). The paper does not adequately explain why the same retrieval mechanism helps dramatically in some settings and hurts in others, weakening the claim of a general retrieval-augmented framework.

Only 3 random seeds with no statistical significance testing; several key comparisons (e.g., MuJoCo improvements of ~1-3 points) are within or near the reported standard errors, and some reported errors (e.g., ±0.02 in Table 2) are suspiciously small for RL evaluation.

The retrieval design is environment-specific and somewhat ad hoc: cosine similarity over raw state features for locomotion, 2D Euclidean position for navigation. It is unclear how the approach scales to high-dimensional observations (images) or realistic robotics settings; all evaluations are on low-dimensional state benchmarks.

Many environment-specific hyperparameters (per-environment planning horizons in Table 6, task-specific 'expert' filtering thresholds, δ, k, η) suggest nontrivial tuning, and the sensitivity of results to these choices is only partially characterized (Tables 9-10 show large swings, e.g., Kitchen-M scores of 0.0 to 72.7 across δ).

The central 'generalization' claim is qualified by the method's own admitted dependence on dataset coverage; the paper frames RAD as addressing OOD states, but in the strictest tests (AntMaze-Large, 0% coverage) the method also fails (0.0), so the improvement is in degree rather than in kind over baselines.
